cards.title: Choose the Right Pop-Up Offer Based on Average Order Value
cards.summary: Offers must be worth exchanging an email for; use percentage discounts below ~$100 AOV, dollar amounts above ~$100, and creative non-discount offers otherwise.
cards.use_when: Selecting or testing the incentive on your pop-up when opt-in rate is low or you are setting up a new form.

cards.title: Run the 5-Step Pop-Up Build Process and a 7-Test Roadmap
cards.summary: Build pop-ups by establishing the offer, choosing form type, creating the form, running a checklist, then AB testing and iterating — expecting many tests before reaching ~10%.
cards.use_when: Standing up a new pop-up program or optimizing an existing form toward 8–12% opt-in.

cards.title: Design the offer before you design the popup
cards.summary: A popup form only converts when the incentive behind it is genuinely worth opting in for, so define a strong offer first and pick the form type second.
cards.use_when: You are planning a list-growth popup (email/SMS capture) and need to decide what incentive to put behind it before building anything.

cards.title: Micro-commit popups: ask a yes/no question before requesting the email
cards.summary: Adding a one-question commit step in front of the email field leverages consistency bias and can lift submit rates versus asking for the email immediately.
cards.use_when: You are building a capture popup and want a low-effort form variant to test against a straight-to-email classic form.

cards.title: Quiz and gamified popups as alternative capture formats
cards.summary: Quizzes trade a question for the discount and can convert better while collecting segmentation data; spin-to-win and reveal-the-discount forms convert strongly but read as tacky.
cards.use_when: You have already tested classic and micro-commit popups and want additional capture formats, or you need customer preference data for future segmentation.

cards.title: Hide the X and force a claim-or-decline decision
cards.summary: Making the close button invisible or replacing it with a visible 'no thanks' option forces shoppers to consciously decide on the offer instead of reflex-closing the popup.
cards.use_when: You are designing a popup whose current form is being reflex-closed in the top corner without the offer being read.

cards.title: Mobile popup build: single-step capture with email then SMS as a separate step
cards.summary: A high-converting mobile popup keeps one input per step, telegraphs the offer, and sequences email capture before SMS rather than stacking both fields together.
cards.use_when: You are configuring a mobile capture popup in your ESP and want a concrete layout order and settings to start from.

cards.title: Desktop popup design: go bigger, use a side image, keep one offer
cards.summary: On desktop, a larger popup with a product image on the side and a single clear offer generally converts better than fly-outs or small embeds, at some cost to shopping experience.
cards.use_when: You are designing the desktop version of a capture popup and deciding on size, layout and imagery.

cards.title: Form targeting: delay, frequency and avoiding exit-intent
cards.summary: Fire popups on a time delay roughly 4-12 seconds after arrival, set a multi-day suppression window after a close, and avoid showing immediately or relying on exit intent.
cards.use_when: You are setting the trigger and frequency rules for a popup and deciding when it appears and re-appears.

cards.title: Popup form QA checklist before launch
cards.summary: A short pre-launch checklist covering inputs per step, timing, load speed, size, copy length, offer prominence and close-button design catches the common conversion killers.
cards.use_when: You have built a popup and are about to publish it; use this to catch obvious issues before sending traffic.

cards.title: Seven A/B tests to run on popup forms, in rough priority order
cards.summary: Test offer first, then form type, close functionality, time delay, imagery, copy and color — but judge delay tests on total submits rather than conversion rate.
cards.use_when: You have a live popup form and need a testing backlog ordered by likely impact on subscriber volume and revenue.

cards.title: Popup platform choice: built-in ESP forms versus a specialist tool
cards.summary: Your ESP's native popup builder is usually good enough to start, but a dedicated popup platform typically performs better at an added monthly cost.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to build capture forms inside your email platform or subscribe to a dedicated popup tool.

cards.title: Flows versus campaigns: what each is for and how to split revenue
cards.summary: Flows fire automatically when a shopper completes a trigger action and handle personalization across the journey; campaigns are manual sends to the list.
cards.use_when: You are planning your email program structure and deciding how much revenue to expect from automated sequences versus one-off sends.

cards.title: The six baseline flows to build first, in order
cards.summary: Nail the basics — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before investing in advanced cross-sell or upsell automations.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which automated email flows to build or fix next, and whether to invest in advanced segmentation or upsell logic.

cards.title: Build flows in a mobile-first multi-step pattern you can clone across devices
cards.summary: Build the mobile popup first, clone it for desktop, and keep each step focused on one input so both versions can be measured separately.
cards.use_when: You are implementing capture forms across device types and want a repeatable build process rather than two independent designs.

cards.title: Prioritize core lifecycle flows over advanced segmentation
cards.summary: Build the seven basic email flows — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before advanced segmentations.
cards.use_when: Planning your store's email lifecycle roadmap or deciding where to invest automation effort first.

cards.title: Welcome flow: 8-email structure with exit filter
cards.summary: A 4-10 email welcome series delivering your acquisition discount, brand story, hero products and social proof, with a purchase filter removing buyers mid-flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up the new-subscriber welcome automation after your popup/form captures an email.

cards.title: Welcome flow's two acceptable outcomes
cards.summary: Design the welcome flow to either convert the curious subscriber or prime a future buyer whose objections are already answered.
cards.use_when: Setting success metrics and email content priorities for the welcome automation.

cards.title: Site abandon flow: one-email nudge to keep browsing
cards.summary: A single email sent 2-4 hours after a site visit with no product view, aimed at re-engaging or routing visitors down the funnel.
cards.use_when: Adding a recovery flow for visitors who hit your homepage or category pages and leave without viewing a product.

cards.title: Browse abandon flow: 5-email recap that escalates slowly
cards.summary: A 5-email sequence for product viewers who didn't add to cart or buy, starting with a fast reminder and saving discounts for later.
cards.use_when: Building the browse-abandonment automation for shoppers who viewed a PDP but didn't add to cart.

cards.title: Cart abandon and checkout abandon are two separate flows
cards.summary: Add-to-cart and checkout-start abandonment need distinct triggers and exit filters, even if they reuse the same email content.
cards.use_when: Auditing or building cart and checkout recovery automations.

cards.title: Cart/checkout abandon content sequence
cards.summary: Email-by-email content plan for cart and checkout abandonment that ends with tiered offers for first-time versus returning buyers.
cards.use_when: Writing the emails inside cart-abandon and checkout-abandon flows.

cards.title: Post-purchase flow: 3 emails that thank, bond, and enable
cards.summary: A short post-purchase sequence: immediate founder thank-you with add-on offer, social follow, then product-usage tips that drive repeat purchase.
cards.use_when: Building the automation that fires immediately after an order is placed.

cards.title: Win-back flow: fire at double the average repurchase interval
cards.summary: A simple 3-email re-engagement sequence timed at roughly twice the customer's average time between purchases.
cards.use_when: Setting up reactivation automation for customers who bought months ago.

cards.title: Use campaigns as the testing ground for flow content
cards.summary: Rather than running many A/B tests inside flows, test angles in frequent campaigns and port winning emails into flows.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to optimize lifecycle emails when flow testing is slow and hard to track.

cards.title: Test flow time delays before content
cards.summary: Time delay from customer action to first email is described as the biggest, fastest lever in flow testing.
cards.use_when: Choosing and tuning send delays for site, browse, cart and checkout abandon flows.

cards.title: Long-form versus short-form flow emails
cards.summary: Test whether abandonment emails should walk through objections or just remind — short reminders often win on impulse purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding email length and content depth in abandonment flows and campaigns.

cards.title: Subject line and preview text tests to run
cards.summary: Specific subject-line variables worth A/B testing: discounts mentioned, emojis, ellipses, caps, and length.
cards.use_when: Running subject line experiments for campaigns or flow emails.

cards.title: Graphic-heavy versus text-based email design
cards.summary: Text-based founder-style emails often outperform graphic-heavy ones, but the source says to balance and test.
cards.use_when: Choosing email format for flow emails such as founder nudges, thank-yous and last-chance messages.

cards.title: Promoting categories versus individual products in email
cards.summary: Test category-level promotion against specific-product promotion — higher-ticket stores in the source leaned toward categories.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to feature in campaign and flow email blocks, especially for higher-ticket catalogs.

cards.title: Seed welcome-flow social proof with early testimonials
cards.summary: Use whatever review volume and testimonials you have, and place them where the sequence's doubts peak.
cards.use_when: Writing welcome-flow emails when you have a new or small brand with little social proof.

cards.title: Founder-message emails and when they convert
cards.summary: Persona-driven 'note from the founder' emails work across welcome, abandonment and win-back flows when kept simple and human.
cards.use_when: Writing personal-voice emails for welcome close, cart abandon, post-purchase thanks or win-back final send.

cards.title: Customize flows with dynamic product blocks
cards.summary: Use platform dynamic content so recovery and recommendation emails show the exact product or a personalized suggestion per recipient.
cards.use_when: Building browse-abandon, cart-abandon, post-purchase and win-back emails in Klaviyo or a comparable platform.

cards.title: Run 3-4 email campaigns per week to carry retention
cards.summary: Regular campaigns, not just flows, drive most repeat purchases; keep send frequency at least two per week.
cards.use_when: Planning weekly retention calendar and deciding how much to rely on automation versus broadcasts.

cards.title: Risk reversal and urgency placement in sequence
cards.summary: Place urgency and risk reversals at the sequence point where they resolve the remaining objection, not in the first email.
cards.use_when: Ordering content in welcome, browse, cart and checkout abandonment sequences.

cards.title: Why the welcome flow exists: email as the cheap way across the trust threshold
cards.summary: Use the welcome flow to send trust-building content at scale, because paid traffic alone makes a first-time buyer too expensive.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget and effort to put into the post-signup welcome flow versus buying more ad impressions.

cards.title: Set the welcome flow length and goal by price point and buying cycle
cards.summary: Run the welcome sequence over 7-14 days for typical AOV, stretching to months for high-ticket products with long consideration.
cards.use_when: Scoping how many emails and how many days your welcome/onboarding flow should cover before you write it.

cards.title: Split dense welcome emails into short, skimmable, spread-out messages
cards.summary: Fix short-but-crammed welcome flows by cutting information per email and spreading it across more emails.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing welcome flow that crams brand story, bestsellers, FAQ and offer into 2-3 long emails.

cards.title: Email 1: deliver the incentive and prove legitimacy in the first screen
cards.summary: Open the welcome flow with a fast, purpose-built email that hands over the discount and gives enough proof to click now.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting the first email a new subscriber receives after opting in.

cards.title: Email 2: put a face to the brand to convert skeptical new signups
cards.summary: Use the brand-story email to humanise the store and address the 'who are these people, are they real' objection.
cards.use_when: Building the second email in the welcome flow for a store that customers find through ads and don't recognise.

cards.title: Email 3: use a bestseller email to collapse choice paralysis
cards.summary: Spotlight one or a few bestsellers with reasons, so undecided buyers don't have to choose between your whole catalogue.
cards.use_when: Designing the mid-flow email for a store with a large catalogue where new subscribers don't know what to buy.

cards.title: Email 4: add urgency plus risk reversal to push the fence-sitters
cards.summary: Turn the coupon reminder into a decision email by combining time pressure, testimonials and guarantees.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer-reminder email mid-flow when subscribers are informed but still not purchasing.

cards.title: Email 5: answer 'why you instead of the competitor' head-on
cards.summary: Use a direct comparison email to let shoppers evaluate you against alternatives and conclude you win.
cards.use_when: Building the comparison email for a crowded niche where buyers are weighing several similar brands.

cards.title: Email 6: dedicate a whole email to social proof
cards.summary: Use one email purely for testimonials, reviews and media mentions to certify that your brand and products are legitimate.
cards.use_when: Building the trust email in the welcome flow, especially for new or unfamiliar brands.

cards.title: Emails 7-8: close with hard urgency, then a founder's personal note
cards.summary: Finish the flow with a last-chance discount email followed by a plain-text founder message extending the offer and inviting replies.
cards.use_when: Writing the final two emails of a welcome flow, for subscribers who have received the whole sequence without buying.

cards.title: Configure the Clavio trigger and filter so buyers drop out of the flow
cards.summary: Install the welcome flow with a signup trigger and a zero-purchases filter so existing and new buyers don't keep receiving sales emails.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automation behind your welcome/onboarding email sequence.

cards.title: Give the welcome flow a target conversion rate and a testing loop
cards.summary: Judge and improve the flow against a realistic conversion band, then compound gains with continuous A/B tests.
cards.use_when: Reviewing welcome flow performance or deciding whether to invest in optimisation work.

cards.title: Reuse winning campaigns as welcome-flow emails to save build time
cards.summary: Monitor your regular campaigns and insert proven ones into the welcome flow with a first-order code added.
cards.use_when: Optimising the welcome flow when you have limited time to write new emails.

cards.title: Audit whether you actually have an abandoned cart flow (added-to-cart vs checkout started)
cards.summary: Most stores think they run an abandoned cart flow but the trigger is actually 'checkout started', leaving the much larger added-to-cart audience untracked and unrecovered.
cards.use_when: Auditing or rebuilding your cart/checkout recovery setup, or when your existing 'abandoned cart' flow underperforms despite being live.

cards.title: Why abandonment is so high and why recovery is high-leverage
cards.summary: 70-85% of carts are abandoned and 26% of abandoners later buy the same item from a competitor, so an unworked cart flow is cash and market share leaking daily.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in cart/checkout recovery, or building the internal case to prioritize it over other store work.

cards.title: Design the recovery flow around the customer's decision cycle, not 1-2 emails
cards.summary: A short recovery flow lets customers off the hook before they finish their real multi-day decision cycle, so extend it to a long, spread-out series with branching.
cards.use_when: Planning the length, spacing, and branching of an abandoned cart/checkout email sequence.

cards.title: Write plain, item-first recovery copy that overcomes objections
cards.summary: Recovery emails should skip fluff and let the dynamic display of the actual abandoned item carry the sale, with copy aimed only at removing uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for any abandoned cart or checkout email.

cards.title: Conversion-optimized recovery email layout
cards.summary: Recovery email designs should be short and focused, with a clear headline, an immediately visible CTA, the abandoned item with details, and trust/reassurance elements.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing the template/layout for abandoned cart and checkout emails.

cards.title: Email 1: the 30-minute quick reminder
cards.summary: The first recovery email is a near-pure reminder that shows the abandoned item and gets the warm, distracted customer over the edge.
cards.use_when: Setting up the first message and its send delay in a cart/checkout recovery flow.

cards.title: Email 2: second reminder with expanded social proof
cards.summary: The follow-up reminder repeats the simple format but leans harder on social proof and risk reversal to catch people who needed another look or were waiting on a paycheck.
cards.use_when: Writing the second message in a recovery flow, roughly a day after the first.

cards.title: Emails 3-4: split by product for specific info, then specific testimonials
cards.summary: Branch the flow by the abandoned product to deliver product-specific information and then product-specific testimonials, which the source says convert skeptical customers better than generic proof.
cards.use_when: Building branching logic in the flow and creating product/collection-specific recovery content.

cards.title: Email 5: last-chance urgency email
cards.summary: Once the customer has all the info, send a sparse urgency email with a hard deadline to push an impulse order, and reopen shopping to other options.
cards.use_when: Writing the mid-to-late recovery email that precedes the discount/support branch.

cards.title: Email 6A: buyer branch — founder support email, no discount
cards.summary: For customers who have bought before, send a personal founder touch offering support and a final chance instead of a discount.
cards.use_when: Configuring the prior-purchase branch in a recovery flow and writing the no-discount variant.

cards.title: Email 6B: discount opener for first-time buyers, then a discount last-chance
cards.summary: For non-buyers, offer a simple flash discount with urgency, then follow with a discount last-chance email; keep both extremely simple and focused on the offer and the abandoned items.
cards.use_when: Setting up the non-buyer branch of a recovery flow that uses a discount to acquire first-time customers.

cards.title: Install the added-to-cart metric and trigger in Klaviyo
cards.summary: The added-to-cart event requires a two-step manual install (snippet on site, then verify in Klaviyo) because it is not added automatically like checkout-started.
cards.use_when: Setting up or troubleshooting a true abandoned cart flow that captures add-to-cart abandoners.

cards.title: Set up dynamic abandoned-item content (careful: cart and checkout variables differ)
cards.summary: Dynamic product sections are the core of recovery emails, but the added-to-cart and checkout-started variables are different, so content built for one won't work in the other.
cards.use_when: Building the item-display block in recovery emails and troubleshooting broken/altered images or links.

cards.title: Set up A/B tests inside the flow rather than on the email
cards.summary: The source prefers a conditional random-sample split within the Klaviyo flow over Klaviyo's built-in email test, because numbers are visible in the flow at a glance.
cards.use_when: Running experiments on recovery emails and wanting quick visibility into results.

cards.title: Small A/B tests can compound into large revenue gains
cards.summary: The source argues small, iterative A/B tests on recovery emails (subject lines, format, layout) can each add meaningful revenue that compounds, so the outline is only a starting point.
cards.use_when: Planning an ongoing optimization cadence for cart/checkout flows after initial launch.

cards.title: Separate cart and checkout flows to avoid double-messaging
cards.summary: Because added-to-cart and checkout-started are different funnel events, you need two flows with exclusion filters so people aren't messaged twice or dropped from the wrong sequence.
cards.use_when: Configuring the triggers and filters of both recovery flows in Klaviyo.

cards.title: Adapt to the 2024 more-competitive buyer who does due diligence
cards.summary: With more stores and a warier, thinner-walleted buyer who shops around, recovery messaging must overcome distrust and comparison shopping, not just remind.
cards.use_when: Setting the tone and content strategy of recovery and lifecycle messaging in a crowded niche.

cards.title: Build a six-email post-purchase flow with timed emotional beats
cards.summary: Six-email post-purchase sequence timed to the buying window, mixing founder gratitude, upsell, and product education to lift repeat purchases without heavy discounting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or rebuilding the post-purchase email flow for your store (replenishment/retention), especially if you currently only send an order confirmation and shipping notice.

cards.title: Exploit the 3-hour post-purchase buyer window
cards.summary: New buyers are far more likely to buy again within hours of ordering, so the first post-purchase email should arrive immediately with an add-on invitation.
cards.use_when: Designing the very first post-purchase email or deciding how aggressive to be with an immediate upsell after checkout.

cards.title: Use founder-voice emails to build small-brand trust after purchase
cards.summary: Plain text founder emails outperform designed ones for post-purchase because they read as genuine and reinforce the 'buy from people' feeling.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy and format for post-purchase gratitude and check-in emails where you want authenticity over polish.

cards.title: Use product-education emails to cut returns and boost repeat orders
cards.summary: Teaching customers how to use what they bought improves their results, which reduces returns and makes them more likely to buy again.
cards.use_when: Writing post-purchase education emails (email 4 in the flow) or building usage guides for products with a learning curve.

cards.title: Set post-purchase email frequency to 3-4 sends per week
cards.summary: The presenter's testing across many frequencies found 3-4 campaigns per week produced the highest revenue with the lowest unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaign emails (not flows) to send per week to your list.

cards.title: Send non-discount content to stay top-of-mind and win repeat purchases
cards.summary: Content that educates and entertains keeps your brand in customers' minds without discounts, priming them to buy when a need arises.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign content for a list you don't want to burn with constant promos, or when trying to protect margins.

cards.title: Structure every email around one micro-topic and one takeaway
cards.summary: Each email should cover one small digestible idea using a micro-topic, so the recipient remembers it in the few seconds they open.
cards.use_when: Choosing what each campaign email should say, or when you feel you have 'nothing to send.'

cards.title: Use the problem-process-solution framework to position your product
cards.summary: Educating on a problem and a process primes the reader so that positioning your product as the solution lands naturally as a purchase.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign emails where you want to sell without an explicit discount, or when introducing a product to skeptical buyers.

cards.title: Generate unlimited micro-topics with a ChatGPT prompt
cards.summary: A single well-structured prompt can produce ~100 micro-topic ideas, enough for a year of non-discount campaign emails.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing your campaign calendar when you need many content ideas quickly.

cards.title: Position email as warm-lead content between cold paid ads and repeat purchases
cards.summary: Email captures attention after paid ads acquire it, then uses cheap content to build trust and drive repeat purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email touchpoints to fund and how email fits with your paid acquisition channels.

cards.title: Understand the trust threshold before asking for a purchase
cards.summary: Customers need multiple exposures to your brand before they trust you enough to buy, so email content exists to accumulate those exposures.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for email campaign performance with skeptical first-time buyers, or diagnosing low conversion from cold traffic.

cards.title: Run A/B tests on flows using the flow-level split, not the email-level test
cards.summary: The presenter recommends testing flow emails by adding a conditional split in the flow builder so results are visible without clicking into the email.
cards.use_when: Setting up an A/B test on an email inside a Klaviyo flow and choosing how to build the test.

cards.title: Add winning campaign emails into your post-purchase flow
cards.summary: Reuse campaign emails that performed well by inserting them into flows, so proof and education content reinforces the purchase.
cards.use_when: Refreshing an existing post-purchase flow, or when you have a strong campaign email (e.g., a research/proof study) you want more mileage from.

cards.title: Use email frequency to build habitual opens and the exposure effect
cards.summary: Frequent, consistent sends create a habit of opening and leverage familiarity to build loyalty and better open rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to send more or less often, or when open rates are declining from infrequent sends.

cards.title: One-Benefit Email Framework
cards.summary: Build repeatable campaigns around a single product benefit so the takeaway sticks in three seconds.
cards.use_when: Planning your monthly email calendar and needing evergreen campaign angles for each product in the store.
